moduleTitle: Shahadah: declaration of faith and its place in Muslim practice

note.specFocus: Know the Shahadah - the declaration of faith - its meaning, Sunni and Shi'a forms, and its place in Muslim practice.
note.summary:
THE WORDS
Sunni Shahadah: 'Ashhadu an la ilaha illa Allah, wa ashhadu anna Muhammadan rasul Allah' - 'I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is the messenger of Allah.'
Many Shi'a Muslims add: 'wa Aliyyun wali Allah' - 'and Ali is the wali (friend/guardian) of Allah', particularly in the adhan. Most Shi'a scholars teach this is recommended (not an obligatory part of the declaration), expressing belief in Imamah.

MEANING
- 'No god but Allah' - Tawhid; rejects shirk (cf. 112:1; 3:18).
- 'Muhammad is the messenger' - Risalah; accepts the Qur'an and Sunnah as final guidance (33:40).
- 'I bear witness' - not just opinion but a public commitment.
- Shahadah literally means 'witnessing/testimony'; the word shahid (witness/martyr) has the same root.

PLACE IN MUSLIM PRACTICE
- First of the Five Pillars for Sunnis ('Islam is built upon five', Bukhari). For Shi'as, it is not one of the Ten Obligatory Acts because belief belongs to Usul ad-Din; the Shahadah expresses Tawhid, Nubuwwah and (with the addition) Imamah.
- Conversion: a person becomes Muslim by sincerely reciting it, usually before witnesses. No other ritual is required. Converts in the UK (often called 'reverts') may say it at a local mosque.
- Birth: the adhan, containing the Shahadah, is whispered into a newborn's right ear, so faith is the first thing a child hears.
- Daily worship: it is in the adhan and iqamah (calls to prayer) and in the tashahhud of every salah, so practising Muslims say it many times a day.
- Death: Muslims hope it will be their last words; relatives recite it at the bedside. The Prophet said one whose last words are 'la ilaha illa Allah' will enter paradise (Abu Dawud).
- Art and symbols: it appears in calligraphy on mosque walls and on flags (e.g. Saudi Arabia).

SINCERITY AND ACTION
The Shahadah must be said with understanding and sincerity (ikhlas); the Qur'an condemns hypocrites who say what is not in their hearts (3:167). Only God knows a person's heart - the Prophet rebuked a man who killed someone who had declared it ('Did you open his heart?', Muslim). It is the gateway to the other pillars: belief shown through action.

EVALUATION THEMES
- Is it the most important pillar? (Foundation of all others vs salah as first thing judged.)
- Is saying it enough to be a 'true' Muslim? (Enters Islam vs lived submission.)
- Is the Shi'a addition acceptable? (Sunnis reject it as an innovation in the adhan; Shi'as see it as an expression of the Prophet's appointment of Ali at Ghadir Khumm.)

KEY TERMS: Shahadah, ashhadu, Tawhid, Risalah, adhan, iqamah, tashahhud, ikhlas, wali.

questions.question:
Which words form the Sunni Shahadah?
A God is greatest; there is no power except with God
B There is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is the messenger of Allah
C In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful
D Glory be to my Lord, the Most High
questions.modelAnswer: B - The Shahadah declares belief in Tawhid and in the prophethood of Muhammad. The other options are other phrases used in worship.
questions.examTip: Read all four options before choosing. Only one letter is credited; if you change your mind, make your final choice clear.

questions.question:
What phrase do many Shi'a Muslims add to the Shahadah, for example in the call to prayer?
A 'and Ali is the wali (friend) of Allah'
B 'and Abu Bakr is the first caliph'
C 'and the Qur'an is created'
D 'and Husayn is the final prophet'
questions.modelAnswer: A - Many Shi'as add 'Ali is the wali of Allah' to express belief in Imamah; most Shi'a scholars regard it as recommended rather than an obligatory part of the Shahadah.
questions.examTip: Read all four options before choosing. Only one letter is credited; if you change your mind, make your final choice clear.

questions.question: Give two occasions when Muslims recite the Shahadah.
questions.modelAnswer: Any two of: in the adhan (call to prayer) whispered into a newborn baby's ear; when converting to Islam (said sincerely before witnesses); as part of daily prayer (in the tashahhud); in the adhan and iqamah before each prayer; ideally as the last words before death; during personal devotion.
questions.examTip: Two brief, accurate points earn the two marks - no development is needed, so don't waste time. Don't give two versions of the same point.

questions.question: Give two beliefs expressed in the Shahadah.
questions.modelAnswer: Any two of: belief in the oneness of God (Tawhid); rejection of any other god (no shirk); belief that Muhammad is a messenger/prophet of God (Risalah); (for Shi'as who add the phrase) belief that Ali is the wali of God (Imamah).
questions.examTip: Two brief, accurate points earn the two marks - no development is needed, so don't waste time. Don't give two versions of the same point.

questions.question: Explain two ways the Shahadah is used in Muslim life.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. It marks the beginning of a Muslim's life. When a baby is born, the father or a relative often whispers the adhan, which contains the Shahadah, into the baby's right ear so that the first words the child hears declare faith in God.

2. It is how a person becomes a Muslim. A convert sincerely recites the Shahadah, usually in front of Muslim witnesses at a mosque. From that moment they are a member of the ummah and take on the duties of the other pillars. Many Muslims also hope it will be the last words they say before death, so family members gently recite it at a dying person's bedside.
questions.examTip: Give two separate ways/beliefs. For each, make the point (1 mark) and then develop it with an example, explanation or consequence (second mark).

questions.question: Explain two reasons why the Shahadah is important to Muslims.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. It summarises the two most important beliefs of Islam - Tawhid and Risalah - in a single sentence. By saying it, a Muslim confirms that only God is worthy of worship and that Muhammad's message must be followed.

2. It is the foundation of the other pillars. Prayer, fasting, zakah and Hajj only have meaning for someone who accepts the Shahadah; it appears in every call to prayer and in the tashahhud of every salah, so Muslims repeat it many times a day as a constant reminder of their commitment.
questions.examTip: Give two separate ways/beliefs. For each, make the point (1 mark) and then develop it with an example, explanation or consequence (second mark).

questions.question:
Explain two Muslim teachings about the meaning of the Shahadah.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Muslim belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. The first part, 'There is no god but Allah', expresses Tawhid and rejects all other objects of worship. It echoes Surah 112: 'Say, He is Allah, the One' (Qur'an 112:1). It means a Muslim must reject shirk in all forms - idols, but also making money or status into a god.

2. The second part, 'Muhammad is the messenger of Allah', expresses Risalah. The Qur'an says 'Muhammad is not the father of any of your men, but he is the Messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets' (Qur'an 33:40). It means Muslims accept the Qur'an revealed through him as final and commit to following his Sunnah. Many Shi'as add 'Ali is the wali of Allah', expressing their belief in the Imamate.
evidence: Qur'an 3:18 ('Allah witnesses that there is no deity except Him')
questions.examTip: Two developed points (2 + 2 marks) plus 1 mark for a relevant, accurate reference to sacred writing or another source of Muslim belief and teaching (Qur'an, Hadith, a scholar, a recognised tradition). One accurate reference is enough; name or paraphrase it clearly.

questions.question:
Explain two reasons why the Shahadah is the first of the Five Pillars.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Muslim belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. It is the declaration of belief on which all other practices depend. The Prophet listed it first: 'Islam is built upon five: testifying that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah…' (Sahih al-Bukhari). Without belief in God and His messenger, prayer, fasting and pilgrimage would have no purpose.

2. It is what makes someone a Muslim. A convert enters Islam by sincerely reciting it, and the Qur'an itself bears witness that 'there is no deity except Him' (Qur'an 3:18). Because it is the entry point into the faith and expresses Tawhid - the most important belief - it naturally comes first and is repeated throughout a Muslim's life, from birth to death.

questions.question:
‘Saying the Shahadah is the most important of the Five Pillars.’
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to Muslim teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS SUPPORTING THE STATEMENT
The Shahadah is the declaration of the two central beliefs of Islam, Tawhid and Risalah, and it is the only pillar that makes someone a Muslim. A convert becomes part of the ummah simply by reciting it sincerely. It is listed first in the hadith 'Islam is built upon five', and every other pillar assumes it: there is no point praying to God or going on pilgrimage to His House if you do not believe in Him. It is also the one pillar no one is exempt from: the sick may be excused fasting, the poor from zakah and Hajj, but every Muslim can say the Shahadah. The Prophet taught that whoever's last words are 'there is no god but Allah' will enter paradise (Abu Dawud), which shows how highly it is valued.

ARGUMENTS AGAINST THE STATEMENT
Others argue that salah is the most important pillar in practice. The Prophet said that 'the first thing a servant will be called to account for on the Day of Judgement is prayer' (Tirmidhi), and salah is performed five times every day, keeping a Muslim constantly aware of God. Words alone are easy to say; the other pillars require sacrifice of time, food and money, and so prove sincerity. The Qur'an repeatedly links belief with action ('those who believe and do righteous deeds'), suggesting the Shahadah is incomplete without the other pillars.

Shi'a Muslims do not list the Shahadah as one of the Ten Obligatory Acts, treating belief as part of Usul ad-Din instead, so for them it cannot be compared directly with the practices. Some Muslims would also say the pillars form a whole and should not be ranked - like pillars of a building, removing any one weakens the structure.

CONCLUSION
Salah and the other pillars are vital ways of living out faith, and saying the Shahadah without meaning it would be worthless. However, the Shahadah's sincere belief is the foundation that gives every other pillar its purpose and is the gateway into Islam. I therefore agree that it is the most important pillar, provided it is understood not just as words but as a lifelong commitment shown through the other pillars.
evidence: Hadith on prayer as first accounted for (Tirmidhi)
questions.examTip: Use the four bullet points as a plan: Muslim teaching, arguments for, arguments against, justified conclusion. Higher levels need logical chains of reasoning and a judgement that weighs the arguments - not just a list. Spelling, punctuation and grammar may also be credited on 12-mark answers.

questions.question:
‘A person only needs to say the Shahadah to be a true Muslim.’
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to Muslim teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS SUPPORTING THE STATEMENT
In Islamic law, a person becomes a Muslim by sincerely reciting the Shahadah; no ceremony, baptism or test is required. The Prophet taught that people should be treated as Muslims if they declare it, and he criticised a Companion who killed a man who had just said it, asking 'Did you open his heart?' (Muslim). Only God can judge what is in a person's heart, so other Muslims should accept anyone who makes the declaration. This reflects God's mercy: anyone, anywhere, can enter Islam simply by believing and saying these words.

ARGUMENTS AGAINST THE STATEMENT
Being a 'true' Muslim means more than saying words. The word 'Muslim' means 'one who submits' to God, and submission is shown in action. The Qur'an warns against hypocrites (munafiqun) who 'say with their mouths what is not in their hearts' (3:167). The Shahadah must be said with sincere belief and understanding, and it brings obligations: performing salah, fasting, giving zakah and, if able, going on Hajj. A hadith teaches that iman has many branches, the highest being the Shahadah and the lowest removing something harmful from a path (Muslim), showing that faith includes actions. Shi'a Muslims would add that a full understanding of faith includes the five roots of Usul ad-Din and the Ten Obligatory Acts, including loyalty to the Ahl al-Bayt.

Many Muslims believe faith increases and decreases with actions, so someone who says the Shahadah but never prays may be a Muslim in name but not living as a 'true' Muslim. On the other hand, most scholars teach that a Muslim who neglects duties out of weakness is still a Muslim, though a sinful one.

CONCLUSION
Saying the Shahadah sincerely is enough to enter Islam, and other people have no right to judge someone's heart. However, the statement is about being a 'true' Muslim, which implies living out the commitment. Since the Qur'an and Hadith link faith closely with action, I disagree with the statement: the Shahadah is the necessary starting point, but a true Muslim also lives by the other pillars and Islamic values.
evidence: Hadith on the branches of faith (Muslim)
